cards.explanation: The answer is that David asks the LORD to arise and come to his aid. He says, “Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid.” Notice who he asks to do the moving, friends. He's asking the LORD to get up and come. (Psalm 35:2)

The answer is that David asks the LORD to tell his soul that He is his salvation. He asks the LORD to say to his soul: “I am your salvation.” Spears are nice, friends, but David wants to hear that one sentence. I think a word like that would settle a worried heart faster than any weapon. (Psalm 35:3)

The answer is the angel of the LORD. David says, “May they be like chaff in the wind, as the angel of the LORD drives them away.” Chaff is the light stuff that blows right off, so it doesn't stand a chance. Nobody argues with wind like that. (Psalm 35:5)

The answer is False. David says they laid their net “without cause” and dug the pit “without reason.” He's not saying they had good reason, friends. He says they had none, and that's exactly why he's crying out. (Psalm 35:7)
The answer is True. David asks, “may the net they hid ensnare them; may they fall into the hazard they created.” The trap they set for him is the one he asks to have catch them, friends. (Psalm 35:8)

The word is rejoice. David says, “Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation.” The fight is loud, friends, but the song ends up somewhere glad. When he's rescued, he knows where the joy goes. (Psalm 35:9)

The answer is True. David's bones say, “Who is like You, O LORD, who delivers the afflicted from the aggressor, the poor and needy from the robber?” He's praising the LORD for delivering the afflicted, the poor and needy. I think David counts himself among them, friends. (Psalm 35:10)
The word is evil. David says, “They repay me evil for good…” He did good, and he got evil back, friends. That's a hard thing to carry, and he says it plainly. (Psalm 35:12)

The answer is False. David says he put on sackcloth and fasted, “…but my prayers returned unanswered.” He doesn't hide it, friends. He just says it, and that honesty is part of why this psalm sticks with people. (Psalm 35:13)

The answer is his friend or brother. David says, “I paced about as for my friend or brother; I was bowed down with grief, like one mourning for his mother.” He grieved the way you grieve for family, friends. That's what makes what comes next hurt so much. (Psalm 35:14)

The answer is that they gathered together in glee. David says, “But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee; they gathered together against me.” When they were ill, he put on sackcloth, and when he stumbled, they gathered against him. Ouch, friends. (Psalm 35:13, 15)

The answer is True. David says, “Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me.” He compares how they acted to godless jesters at a feast, with the teeth grinding. That's a heavy picture, friends, and I think it hurts to read. (Psalm 35:16)

The answer is “How long will You look on.” David asks, “How long, O Lord, will You look on?” It's an honest question, friends, and he brings it straight to the Lord. He doesn't take it anywhere else. (Psalm 35:17)

The answer is in the great assembly. David says, “Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly; I will praise You among many people.” He says he'll give thanks in the great assembly and praise among many people. I think he wants a crowd to hear it, friends. (Psalm 35:18)

The answer is those who live quietly in the land. David says, “For they do not speak peace, but they devise deceitful schemes against those who live quietly in the land.” The people being schemed against are the quiet ones, friends. Folks just minding their own business. (Psalm 35:20)

The answer is “You have seen it.” The enemies say, “Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!” Then David says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent.” He turns to the LORD and says the LORD has seen it, friends. (Psalm 35:21-22)
The word is silent. David says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me.” He wants to hear from the LORD, friends, and he wants Him close. (Psalm 35:22)
The answer is the LORD's righteousness. David says, “Vindicate me by Your righteousness, O LORD my God…” He isn't pointing to his own record, friends. He's pointing to who the LORD is. (Psalm 35:24)

The answer is False. David says, “May those who gloat in my distress be ashamed and confounded; may those who exalt themselves over me be clothed in shame and reproach.” He asks for shame and reproach, not honor. Funny how the ones lifting themselves up get dressed in the opposite, friends. (Psalm 35:26)

The answer is True. David says, “May those who favor my vindication shout for joy and gladness…” He's not alone in this psalm, friends. Some people are on his side, and he wants them shouting. (Psalm 35:27)

The answer is his servant's well-being. David wants them to always say, “Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant’s well-being.” The verse names the servant's well-being as what the LORD delights in, friends. That's a line worth saying always. (Psalm 35:27)

The answer is all day long. David says, “Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long.” After a psalm that starts in the middle of a fight, friends, it ends with praise. I'd say that's a good way to finish. (Psalm 35:28)
